neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Bilateral complete facial paralysis — unable to close either eye, bilateral lagophthalmos with Bell's phenomenon preserved. Unable to clench teeth, frown, show teeth, blow, or whistle. Nasolabial folds absent bilaterally. Drooling. Loss of taste bilaterally. Slurred speech. No ptosis. Pupils equal and reactive. Full extraocular movements. No diplopia.
neurological_exam.motor: Bilateral lower extremity: hip flexion 4/5, knee extension 4+/5 bilaterally. Upper extremity 4+/5.
neurological_exam.reflexes: Diminished deep tendon reflexes throughout — ankle jerks absent bilaterally, patellar and upper extremity 1+.
neurological_exam.gait: Slightly unsteady — can walk with careful monitoring.
neurological_exam.additional: FVC: 3.2 L (predicted 4.4 L — 73%). NIF: -42 cmH2O. No preceding illness, no recent travel, no sick contacts, no insect bites. Bilateral simultaneous facial nerve palsy — bilateral Bell's palsy is rare and should trigger systemic workup.

patient.chief_complaint: One-day sudden-onset bilateral facial paralysis with loss of taste, drooling, and inability to close eyes — no limb weakness.
patient.history_present_illness: Mr. H. is a 36-year-old IT specialist presenting with a 1-day history of sudden-onset bilateral facial paralysis. He awoke this morning unable to close either eye completely, with bilateral drooping of both cheeks, inability to purse his lips, and drooling of saliva. He cannot close his eyes, frown, show his teeth, blow, or whistle. He has lost taste bilaterally and has mild slurring of speech. There is no earache, hearing change, tinnitus, headache, neck stiffness, photophobia, or fever. He has no limb weakness or sensory symptoms. There is no history of recent infection, travel, sick contacts, insect bites, or trauma. He does not smoke, drink alcohol, or use illicit drugs. He has never had a similar episode. His primary care physician initially considered Bell's palsy but was concerned because bilateral simultaneous facial palsy is rare and strongly suggests an underlying systemic process. Bilateral LMN facial palsy (bilateral diplegia) is a classic presenting feature of GBS — occurring in 50% of GBS cases — and requires urgent workup to identify the underlying cause and assess for systemic neuropathy. The finding of globally diminished reflexes on neurological exam, despite the patient's primary complaint being facial, raises the clinical suspicion for a broader peripheral neuropathy.

quantitative_data.pattern: Demyelinating polyneuropathy with prominent bilateral facial nerve involvement — GBS with bilateral facial diplegia presentation

specialized_test.impression: Demyelinating polyneuropathy. Abnormal blink reflex bilaterally — absent R1 and abnormal R2 responses confirming bilateral facial nerve conduction delay. Absent H-reflex. Prolonged F-waves bilaterally. Mildly prolonged distal motor latencies and borderline reduced conduction velocities in limb nerves. Mildly reduced sural SNAP amplitudes. Findings are consistent with a demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy with prominent bilateral cranial nerve involvement. Clinical correlation recommended.

ground_truth.primary_diagnosis: Guillain-Barré syndrome, bilateral facial diplegia variant (cranial GBS), seronegative except low-titer anti-GQ1b

differential.key_features: Bilateral simultaneous idiopathic Bell's palsy is extremely rare (<1:5 million); systemic cause must be excluded; systemic neuropathy and areflexia confirm GBS
Lyme is a major cause of bilateral facial palsy — excluded by negative Lyme ELISA
Normal ACE, no hilar adenopathy on CT chest, no other sarcoid features
No ophthalmoplegia; no ataxia; full extraocular movements; anti-GQ1b low titer only

optimal_actions.action: Urgent eye care — lubricant drops and eye patches for lagophthalmos

critical_actions: Bilateral simultaneous facial palsy is never idiopathic Bell's palsy — always requires systemic workup
Lyme disease is the most common systemic cause of bilateral facial palsy — negative Lyme ELISA is a required first step
Urgent eye protection: lubricant drops and tape/patches to prevent corneal exposure keratopathy from lagophthalmos
Blink reflex study is the NCS test specifically for facial nerve demyelination in GBS
Albumino-cytologic dissociation confirms the GBS diagnosis and excludes infectious meningitis
contraindicated_actions: Corticosteroids (primary treatment — does not work in GBS)
Treating as bilateral Bell's palsy without systemic workup
key_reasoning_points: Bilateral facial diplegia is a classic GBS presentation — occurs in ~50% of GBS cases and can be the presenting symptom before ascending limb weakness develops
Bilateral Bell's palsy is extremely rare as idiopathic entity — systemic workup is mandatory: Lyme, sarcoid, HIV, GBS
Lyme neuroborreliosis is the most common non-GBS cause of bilateral facial palsy in endemic areas — always test first
Diminished reflexes in the limbs (even without overt limb weakness) is the clinical clue that this is systemic GBS not just bilateral cranial neuropathy
Blink reflex study — abnormal R1 bilaterally — is the electrophysiological confirmation of bilateral facial nerve demyelination in GBS

metadata.difficulty_description: Bilateral facial diplegia as presenting GBS manifestation — requires exclusion of Lyme, sarcoid, and intracranial causes; systemic neuropathy confirmed by diminished reflexes
